book.author: Stephen R. Jordan

name: Teacher Planning, Grading, and Feedback
blurb: Fifteen teachers in five primary schools in England used AI to help plan lessons for two school terms. Their self reported weekly planning time fell by 52.5 percent, from about 10 hours to under 5 (Carson et al., 2026).
title: Teacher Planning, Grading, and Feedback
answer: Fifteen teachers in five primary schools in England used AI to help plan lessons for two school terms. Their self reported weekly planning time fell by 52.5 percent, from about 10 hours to under 5 (Carson et al., 2026).

papers.why: Names the division of labor question the book raises in Chapter 11: which parts of a lesson the bot runs and which the teacher runs.
papers.title: A systematic review of conversational AI in language education: focusing on the collaboration with human teachers
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Technology in Education (Taylor and Francis)
papers.caveat: Abstract only, closed access. Language learning only, pre ChatGPT.
papers.finding: Systematic review of 24 studies (2015 to 2021) on conversational AI in language learning. Little evidence of real collaboration between AI and human teachers. Roles of AI and teachers were mapped per learning phase. Authors argue for AI that amplifies teacher intelligence and reduces workload through classroom orchestration, and give guidelines for teachers and AI researchers.

papers.why: Direct evidence for the draft then edit pattern in Chapter 17, and a clear statement that generated plans are a scaffold, not a lesson. The equity angle (open educational resources for under resourced schools) is a strong argument for the book's rural and small school walkthroughs.
papers.title: ChatGPT and Generative AI: Possibilities for Its Contribution to Lesson Planning, Critical Thinking and Openness in Teacher Education
papers.venue: Education Sciences (MDPI)
papers.caveat: One lesson, one subject, one grade, no participants, no classroom trial. The authors say so themselves. Findings are the authors' reading of one output, so nothing here measures learning.
papers.finding: Exploratory document analysis of one ChatGPT generated Grade 6 second language lesson plan on prepositions, plus published teacher reactions to a ChatGPT climate change lesson. The generated plan had every basic element (purpose, warm up, presentation, practice, production, wrap up, assessment) with timing per stage, and teachers agreed it was a usable framework that saved time. Teachers also called it outdated, unsourced, and a recipe that still needs a chef. The authors argue the real value is equity: free, contextualized lesson materials for teachers who lack textbooks or paid resources.

papers.why: The only randomized evidence in the set, and it supports the book's feedback before grades pattern: AI feedback on drafts is worth doing, cheap, and motivating, while learning transfer needs repeated cycles, not one session. The prompt design is a ready made template for Chapter 17.
papers.title: Using LLMs to bring evidence-based feedback into the classroom: AI-generated feedback increases secondary students’ text revision, motivation, and positive emotions
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence (Elsevier)
papers.caveat: One session, one task, grade 10, foreign language writing, no comparison to teacher feedback, and students were not told the feedback came from AI. Feedback quality was not checked per student. Novelty effects cannot be ruled out. Effects on a new task were not significant.
papers.finding: Randomized controlled study, 459 Grade 10 students in German academic track schools, May to June 2023, one 90 minute lesson. Students wrote a TOEFL style argumentative essay in English, then half received GPT-3.5-turbo feedback and half only an instruction to revise. Feedback raised revision quality (d = 0.19), motivation for future writing tasks (d = 0.36), positive emotions (d = 0.34), and perceived usefulness (d = 1.19). It did not raise performance on a new essay written the same day. The prompt followed Hattie and Timperley: hints and examples on structure, content, and language, in a table, quoting the student text, with the model told the writers were upper secondary foreign language learners, temperature 0. Perceived usefulness averaged only 3.7 of 7, so quality has room to improve.

papers.why: Background for AI scoring caution.
papers.title: A framework for evaluation of large language models in essay assessment: Reliability, alignment, and causal reasoning
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Framework evaluating LLM essay assessment for reliability, alignment, and causal reasoning.

papers.why: Feedback type design matters.
papers.title: Directive, metacognitive, or a blend of both? A comparison of AI-generated feedback types on student engagement, confidence, and outcomes
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Compared directive, metacognitive, and blended AI feedback on engagement, confidence, and outcomes.

papers.why: Supports process-based assessment redesign.
papers.title: Coauthorship integrity: Reconceptualising assessment validity for the age of generative artificial intelligence
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Reframes assessment validity around co-authorship with GenAI.

papers.why: AI can flag explicit lesson plan features but not judge quality alone.
papers.title: How reliable are large language models in analyzing the quality of written lesson plans? A mixed-methods study from a teacher internship program
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: ChatGPT-o1 rated 32 long pre-service lesson plans against experts: moderate reliability (alpha .69, 73.8% exact agreement); struggled with implicit and contextual quality.

papers.why: Background.
papers.title: Optimizing automated scoring in ILSAs with prompt compression
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Prompt compression for automated scoring in international large-scale assessments.

papers.why: Time savings are real but get eaten by other work unless leaders protect them.
papers.title: Embedding AI in Lesson Planning
papers.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on Networked Learning
papers.finding: 15 teachers in five English primary schools over two terms: self-reported weekly planning time fell 52.5% (10 to 4.75 hours); saved time was often absorbed by other demands.

papers.why: Gives a concrete classroom routine for AI feedback.
papers.title: Stop perfecting the feedback, start supporting the uptake: rethinking AI in writing instruction
papers.venue: Frontiers in Education
papers.finding: Argues AI feedback uptake is low in K-12 and proposes a five-phase model: draft, AI feedback, individual revision, peer discussion, whole-class reflection with teacher as facilitator.

papers.why: Supports no AI-only grading.
papers.title: Opening the blackbox of LLM-based automated essay scoring: Insights into feature weighting patterns and score validity
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: LLM automated essay scoring feature weighting differs from human rubric priorities, raising score validity concerns.

papers.why: AI feedback's value is redistributing teacher effort, not beating teachers.
papers.title: Comparing Teacher and AI-Generated Feedback in the Writing Classroom: Experimental Results from Secondary School Classrooms
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Thirteenth ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale
papers.caveat: Two sessions, feedback given once; immediate condition confounded with same-session second task; prompt did not include praise; sample may be underpowered per authors.
papers.finding: Within-class randomized trial, German grades 10-11 EFL writing (N=391): teacher-written feedback vs delayed GPT-4 feedback vs immediate GPT-4 feedback. No significant differences in revision performance, second-task performance, or revision time. Bayesian analysis: teacher feedback likely slightly better for transfer to a second task and for how positive feedback felt. Immediate AI feedback was rated more useful and more motivating. Immediacy alone did not improve performance.

papers.why: Source labels bias students' judgment of feedback.
papers.title: Can students judge like experts? A large-scale study on the pedagogical quality of AI and human personalized formative feedback
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: 979 feedback pieces: AI and human formative feedback had comparable pedagogical quality; both weak on metacognition. 472 STEM students judged feedback by who they believed wrote it, not its actual quality.

papers.why: Feedback that is not used does nothing; uptake must be designed into lessons.
papers.title: Feedback from Generative AI: Correlates of Student Engagement in Text Revision from 655 Classes from Primary and Secondary School
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
papers.caveat: Vendor trial data, no student demographics or prompt; engagement is a one-character proxy; novelty of a new tool may cut either way.
papers.finding: Commercial GenAI (GPT-4) feedback platform, Germany, Nov 2023: 655 teacher-designed tasks, 14,236 students, grades 1-12. 48% (6,889) did not change a single character after feedback. Rates were flat across grade bands (primary 48% engaged, grades 5-6 49%, 7-9 51%, 10-11 52%, upper secondary 51%), task types (47-51%), and languages. No linguistic feature of drafts or feedback predicted engagement. Only 20 of 655 classes had every student revise; 27 had none.

papers.title: Evaluating Language Models Using Linguistic Variations in Multilingual Learners' Writing: A Teacher Study
papers.venue: International Conference of the Learning Sciences
papers.finding: Teachers found a multilingual language model misread common linguistic variations in multilingual learners' writing.

papers.why: Bias depends on detector design; public tools differ from purpose-built ones.
papers.title: Detecting ChatGPT-generated essays in a large-scale writing assessment: Is there a bias against non-native English speakers?
papers.venue: Computers & Education
papers.finding: Custom detectors built on GRE data showed near-perfect accuracy and no bias against non-native speakers.

papers.why: Concrete example of why AI lesson plans need teacher checking.
papers.title: Opportunities and risks involved in using ChatGPT to create first grade science lesson plans
papers.venue: PLOS ONE
papers.finding: Case study: a first grade science lesson plan was generated and refined in 30 minutes, aligned to 5E, but contained questionable parts, missing details, and a fake resource.

papers.why: Feedback works best when turned into a few personal revision goals.
papers.title: Individualizing goal-setting interventions using automated writing evaluation to support secondary school students’ text revisions
papers.venue: Learning and Instruction
papers.finding: 345 German upper secondary ESL students: individualized goal-setting based on automated writing evaluation scores produced the largest revision gains.

papers.why: Weak evidence that AI-planned lessons matter for outcomes.
papers.title: Are Lesson Plans Created by ChatGPT More Effective? An Experimental Study
papers.venue: International Journal of Technology in Education
papers.finding: 39 third graders: lessons from ChatGPT-assisted plans raised achievement, but the difference from control was not significant.

papers.why: Teachers remain better; AI fits early drafts.
papers.title: Comparing the quality of human and ChatGPT feedback of students’ writing
papers.venue: Learning and Instruction
papers.finding: 200 human vs 200 ChatGPT feedback pieces on secondary essays: trained humans gave higher-quality feedback in all categories except criteria-based; AI may help for early drafts.

papers.why: Clear division of labor between teacher and AI.
papers.title: Large language models in education: A focus on the complementary relationship between human teachers and ChatGPT
papers.venue: Education and Information Technologies
papers.finding: Eleven language teachers used ChatGPT for two weeks. AI roles: interlocutor, content provider, teaching assistant, evaluator. Teacher roles: orchestrating resources, making students investigators, raising AI ethics awareness.

papers.why: Solid pre-GenAI evidence for automated writing feedback.
papers.title: Automated feedback and writing: a multi-level meta-analysis of effects on students' performance
papers.venue: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence
papers.finding: Meta-analysis of 20 studies (N=2,828): automated writing feedback had a medium effect (g=0.55) on writing performance, with high heterogeneity.

papers.why: Detectors are unfair to English learners; never use them as sole evidence.
papers.title: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers
papers.venue: Patterns
papers.finding: GPT detectors frequently misclassify non-native English writing as AI-generated.

papers.why: Strategy feedback matters more than surface fixes.
papers.title: Automated writing evaluation: Does spelling and grammar feedback support high-quality writing and revision?
papers.venue: Assessing Writing
papers.finding: 119 high school students: strategy feedback plus revision improved essays; spelling and grammar checkers added small gains on some subscales.

papers.why: Shows districts can pool item banks for adaptive testing.
papers.title: The development and implementation of a computer adaptive progress test across European countries
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Consortium of 8 European medical schools built a shared computer adaptive progress test.

papers.why: Tells buyers to ask what a tool adapts feedback to and why.
papers.title: Personalized feedback in digital learning environments: Classification framework and literature review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Review of 39 studies on personalized feedback in K-12 and higher ed. Feedback is mostly adapted only to current knowledge and behavior; few studies justify why a message goes to a given student. Most report positive, mixed, or neutral effects.

papers.why: Frames why assessment redesign is part of AI adoption, not just cheating prevention.
papers.title: Assessment in the age of artificial intelligence
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Position paper: traditional assessment is hard to design, gives snapshots, is not adapted to learners, fits school culture more than real-world culture, and tests skills humans now do with computers. Reviews AI approaches that partly address this and their new challenges.

papers.why: Simple, explainable diagnostic idea (fast/slow x right/wrong) that any quiz platform can show students.
papers.title: An interactive test dashboard with diagnosis and feedback mechanisms to facilitate learning performance
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Two classes, one unit, not randomized.
papers.finding: Quasi-experiment, 50 Grade 8 physics students in Taiwan. Dashboard used response time plus correctness to tag each concept as skilled, understood but slow, not understood, or guessing. Experimental class beat control on learning, physics self-efficacy, and technology acceptance; learning gains held for high and low prior knowledge.

papers.why: Important nuance: automatic feedback helps students more reliably than it saves teacher time. Set expectations for time savings honestly.
papers.title: Automatic feedback in online learning environments: A systematic literature review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Mostly higher ed online courses and pre-generative systems.
papers.finding: Review of 63 studies. 65% show automatic feedback improves student performance; 46% found no evidence it eases instructor workload; 83% found no evidence manual feedback beats automatic. Main method compares answers to a model answer.

children.name: Lesson Plans and Units
children.blurb: AI can draft a first version of a lesson plan or unit map in minutes, which saves teachers time but does not replace their judgment.

children.name: Differentiated Materials
children.blurb: Differentiated materials is the practice of using AI to produce several versions of the same lesson, worksheet, or reading passage at different levels of support, while the teacher makes sure every version still teaches the same core content.

children.name: Emergency Substitute Plans
children.blurb: Emergency substitute plans are ready-made lesson plans a teacher keeps on hand for unexpected absences, drafted with AI help so a stranger can follow them.

children.name: Feedback Students Actually Use
children.blurb: Feedback Students Actually Use is the idea that giving more feedback only matters if students act on it, and that AI can help teachers produce more feedback but not necessarily better feedback.

children.name: Building Revision Into Class
children.blurb: Building revision into class means making revision a planned, guided part of the lesson rather than an optional extra.

children.name: No AI Only Grades
children.blurb: No AI Only Grades means that every grade a student receives must be a decision made and confirmed by a teacher, never assigned by an AI tool on its own.

children.name: Grading Calibration
children.blurb: Grading calibration is the practice of teachers who share a course scoring the same samples of student work together and discussing their differences so that a student's grade does not depend on which teacher they happen to have.

children.name: Plagiarism and AI Detection
children.blurb: AI detection tools are unreliable and often misclassify writing by non native English speakers as AI generated, so a detection flag should never by itself lead to a penalty.

children.name: Planning Together
children.blurb: Planning together means teachers on a team use AI to draft shared materials, then review and revise them as a group.

children.name: Student Work and Privacy
children.blurb: Student work such as essays, projects, and test answers counts as part of a student's education record, so pasting it into a general chat tool shares that record with a company the district has no agreement with.

children.name: Report Cards and Parent Emails
children.blurb: AI can help teachers draft report card comments, parent emails, recommendation letters, PLC agendas and seating charts, but the teacher must supply the specific substance and revise every draft so it sounds like them and reflects the real student.

children.name: The Time Study: Is AI Actually Saving Time?
children.blurb: A time study checks whether an AI tool actually saves teachers time by measuring how long key tasks took before the tool and how long they take after, including the time spent checking and correcting AI output.

children.name: Protecting the Time Saved
children.blurb: Protecting the time saved means that school leaders deliberately decide where the hours AI frees up for teachers will go, rather than letting them disappear into new meetings, forms, and duties.

children.name: New Teachers and AI
children.blurb: New teachers can use AI to produce plans and materials faster, easing the pressure of their first years, but planning is a skill that develops through doing it.

children.name: When Not to Use AI
children.blurb: Some teaching moments should stay entirely with the teacher, including personal conversations with students, feedback on deeply personal writing, and decisions about grades or placement.

sections.body: This section of school life covers the work teachers do around lessons: planning units and single lessons, making materials for different learners, giving feedback on student writing, grading, checking for plagiarism, writing reports and messages to parents, and keeping track of whether any of it is actually faster. The book describes AI being used to draft lesson plans, generate differentiated versions of materials, produce feedback on essays, score writing, and help with communication. It reports that fifteen teachers in five English primary schools used AI for planning across two terms and their self reported weekly planning time fell from about ten hours to under five. It also notes that a first grade science plan made with AI in thirty minutes followed a sound teaching model but had questionable content, missing details, and a resource that did not exist. The book's frame is that speed is encouraging but quality and where the saved time goes are what matter.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, as the book finds it, is AI as a drafting aid that a teacher then checks and edits, which it calls the draft then edit habit and the foundation of the whole chapter. What does not work is using AI output unchecked, because drafts can carry errors, and treating saved hours as a win when those hours get absorbed by other demands, which the book calls the vanishing hour. It also holds that detection scores are never proof on their own and never lead to penalties alone, and that no grade is assigned by AI alone. The rule the book holds to is that the teacher signs every grade and that saved time must be deliberately protected and directed, otherwise nothing that matters has changed. It adds that a district without a measure of time saved is paying for promises.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from the daily work outward to the rules and the measurement. A teacher would start with Lesson Plans and Units and Differentiated Materials for the core planning tasks, then Emergency Substitute Plans for the case where a plan is needed fast, and New Teachers and AI for the same tasks at the start of a career. For the feedback side, Feedback Students Actually Use and Building Revision Into Class sit with Grading Calibration, while No AI Only Grades and Plagiarism and AI Detection carry the rules about who decides a grade and what a detection score may never do. Planning Together, Student Work and Privacy, and Report Cards and Parent Emails cover the shared and outward facing parts of the work, and When Not to Use AI marks the limits. A leader or board member would go to The Time Study: Is AI Actually Saving Time? for the evidence question and Protecting the Time Saved for what to do with the hours once they are found.
sections.heading: How these pages fit together
